title: Chapter 7 — Of The Cause Of A Leaning To Pantheism Amongst Democratic Nations
paragraphs: I shall have occasion later to show in what form the dominant taste of a democratic people for very general ideas shows itself in politics. But at this stage of my work I want to point out its principal effect on philosophy. It cannot be denied that pantheism has made great progress in our age. The writings of part of Europe bear visible marks of it: the Germans introduce it into philosophy, and the French into literature. Most of the works of imagination published in France contain some opinions, or some tinge, taken from pantheistic doctrines, or show in their authors some leaning toward such doctrines. This seems to me to come not from an accidental cause but from a permanent one.

When the conditions of society are becoming more equal, and each individual becomes more like all the rest, weaker and more insignificant, a habit grows up of no longer noticing citizens in order to consider only the people, and of overlooking individuals in order to think only of their kind. At such times the human mind seeks to take in a multitude of different objects at once, and it constantly strives to link a variety of effects to a single cause. The idea of unity takes such hold of a person, and he seeks it so universally, that if he thinks he has found it, he readily settles down to rest in that belief. Nor is he content with the discovery that there is nothing in the world but a creation and a Creator. Still troubled by this first division of things, he tries to broaden and simplify his conception by including God and the universe in one great whole. Suppose there is a philosophical system that teaches that all things, material and immaterial, visible and invisible, that the world contains are only to be considered as the several parts of one immense Being, which alone stays unchanged amid the continual change and ceaseless transformation of everything that makes it up. We may readily infer that such a system will have secret charms for people living in democracies, even though it destroys the individuality of man, or rather precisely because it destroys that individuality. All their habits of thought prepare them to conceive it and predispose them to adopt it. It naturally attracts and holds their imagination; it feeds the pride of their minds while it soothes their laziness. Among the different systems by which philosophy tries to explain the universe, I believe pantheism to be one of those best fitted to seduce the human mind in democratic ages. All who remain attached to the true greatness of man should struggle against it and unite against it.
